Marathon Petroleum stock has dropped 18.5% over the past two weeks, with today's modest 1.2% decline continuing that slide. The sharpest fall came on November 4th—right after the midterm elections—when crude oil prices tumbled on mixed signals about U.S.-Iran tensions and the potential for diplomatic progress. Oil futures fell despite analyst warnings that renewed conflict could push prices above $100; the market was wrestling with competing risks, and that uncertainty hit refiner valuations hard. Today's small additional decline fits within that broader selloff rather than marking a new shock.

Refineries are running at high capacity (94.5%) with elevated crude in storage (692 million barrels), which limits refiners' pricing power when oil prices weaken. A Democratic Congress could also shift energy policy away from traditional refining and toward renewables, adding longer-term headwinds to the sector that investors are pricing in.
